_comment: Which widget kinds get a TRANSCRIBED EXEMPLAR in WIDGET-SHAPES.json.
scripts/extract-widget-shapes.ts regenerates the asset; --check gates it.
Counts are harvested for EVERY kind the client has delivered — instances,
pages, hosting UITypes, schema versions, settings-key frequency, and the
entry-key frequency of every settings array. `detail` only decides which
kinds also carry a full settings block, because those cost prompt budget.
Filter and Button are here because they are the two shapes we have never
emitted (F-171). Grid, Form and UiPageWidget already have hand-written
shapes in WIDGETS.md, so an exemplar would only duplicate them.
THE COUNTS ARE THE POINT, NOT THE EXEMPLAR. The last time an asset cited a
single example, the model read it as a rule about where the thing belongs
and declined to emit a service call on an ordinary Page (F-172). Adding a
kind here adds one data point INSIDE its own distribution.
How ENTITY-TYPES.md is built (A-16). scripts/build-entity-types.ts regenerates it.
detail = entities whose FULL property list is fed to the model. Everything else
is indexed by name and property count only, so the model knows the entity exists
and can report a gap rather than guessing.
WHY NOT ALL 340 (D-04): the full property text is 246 KB against a ~304 KB cached
prefix — it would nearly double what every request pays to cache. Five entities
cost 17 KB and the index costs 8 KB. Per-story selection was rejected because the
package sits before the single cache breakpoint, so a varying asset would miss the
cache on every first attempt.
Add an entity here when a story needs it, then re-run the script.

only when the key is present here, so the package contents are driven by config rather than
by source. Remove a key to drop its block; add one to introduce another static asset.

_effortNote: SWEPT TWICE, 2026-08-24: xhigh -> high -> medium, each step measured before it
shipped. The original note asked for exactly this once evals existed; they now
do (two scored pairs, a 30-file acceptance corpus, a reproducibility method).
GENERATE, on US-455386 _New, fixed descriptor + --templates-from:
xhigh    205.4s   first token 86.5s   20,562 out   (1 run)
high     151-172s first token 50-59s  ~16,000 out  (3 runs)
medium   119-121s first token 23-29s  ~13,300 out  (3 runs)   <- shipped
low      101.0s   first token 16.2s   11,718 out   (1 run)    <- rejected
=> medium is 41% less wall clock and 70% less time to the first character
than xhigh, and 22% less than high.
EXTRACT, same story, 3 runs at medium against 1 at high:
high    24.2s + 22.7s      medium  19.3s + 22.5s
All 8 structural dimensions of the descriptor IDENTICAL across the three
medium runs AND matching high: pages, uiType, grids with every column's
type and path, forms, buttons, queries, api, queryDefinitions.
QUALITY HELD AT MEDIUM, and this is the reason it shipped rather than the
speed. Every arm scored 24 identical / 5 different against Athena's delivered
page - xhigh, high, medium and low all produced the SAME five differences,
each of which is something the requirement document does not ask for. All
runs passed on attempt 1 at PASS 21 WARN 2 FAIL 0.
MEDIUM IS ALSO MORE REPRODUCIBLE THAN HIGH. Its three runs were identical on
all five functional dimensions including all 13 links. One high run of three
dropped the two `loadChange -> loading` spinner links.
WHY NOT LOW: it saves a further 15% but drops those same two spinner links.
That is the cliff. Not broken, but it is paying quality for a smaller return.
WHAT IS *NOT* THE BOTTLENECK, measured so nobody re-optimises it: the cached
prefix. scripts/cache-probe.ts sends the 161,515-token package twice: writing
it costs 3.8s, reading it 2.6s. Passing the dictionary, skeleton, samples and
OOB pages costs about 3 seconds of a two-minute run. The cost is the model
THINKING - roughly 7,400 of medium's 13,300 output tokens are thinking, and
the emitted JSON is only ~5,900. Effort is the lever; prompt size is not.
Override per run with `--effort <level>` on the generate or PRD CLI. Those
flags are measurement controls, not settings anyone needs day to day.
_streamIdleNote: Seconds a generation may stream without producing a character before it is

the stack could break that: `call()` awaits finalMessage(), a hang throws
nothing, so the retry loop never fired and the HTTP request stayed open.
The threshold has to clear the longest legitimate silence, which is the wait
for the FIRST token, not any mid-stream gap: 23-29s at medium, 50-59s at
high, 86.5s at xhigh, and 49.2s in the run that then hung. 120 is better
than 2x the worst of those and still ends a hang in two minutes instead of

_comment: The UI technology being generated for. This is the seam that keeps the spec
descriptor target-neutral (T-16).
pageTypes are the CLASSES OF SCREEN the target platform recognises. Everything
else in the descriptor is generic UI vocabulary — entity, columns, forms, grids,
actionButtons, filters, joins — but `Cluster` and `Step` are CMF page classes,
not universal concepts, and they were written into src/descriptor.ts as a fixed
enum. That was the last CMF-specific term in the neutral layer.
For CMF these are the four the platform defines, and platform.ts maps each to
its numeric UIType code (0 Page, 1 Step, 2 Wizard, 3 Cluster) measured across
the 66 live pages. A different target declares its own list here and supplies
its own platform module; the descriptor needs no code change.
Remove this block and the descriptor falls back to the CMF four, so an older
config still loads.
Where the client REGISTERS their custom actions (T-31).
An action button needs an actionId and an actionButtonId, and a requirement
document almost never names them. But they are not unknowable: the Angular
customization registers every one, with its button id, title and icon.
This is transcription, not inference. Their own registry holds
Custom.ChangePriorityAction next to CustomActionTransfer.Id next to
Material.Rework - three shapes, no derivable rule. A guessed actionId gives
a button that renders and does nothing when clicked.
Remove this block and the generator falls back to reporting UNKNOWN, exactly
as it did before.

_comment: The .txt copies of the requirement documents are DERIVED, not authored.
scripts/extract-stories.ts writes them through the same documentText() the
application uses, and --check fails when one drifts from its .docx.
They HAD drifted: 14 of 18 were short, by up to 2,748 characters, and what
they were missing was the Word review comments. On US-455386_New those
comments carry two accepted decisions - the Product filter field and the
Traveler Print button - that appear nowhere in the body text. A grep of the
.txt answered a question about them confidently and wrongly.
Roots are searched in order and the first match wins, so put the delivered
originals ahead of any working copy. A .txt with no .docx anywhere is left
alone and reported: several stories were delivered as plain text.

_comment: Where to look for query exports the client has ALREADY delivered, so a story
that merely names a query can still produce one (T-21).
This is transcription, not inference. A query's joins cannot be derived from
its name: ProductionOrder -> Product joins ProductId -> DefinitionId (F-125).
A run that inferred a query body would produce one that executes and returns
the wrong rows — the worst outcome available.
Matching is on the query's OWN <Name>, never on the filename: exports carry
load-order prefixes (100_CustomRetrieveProductionOrders.xml) and the same
query appears under several feature folders.
Empty this list to disable transcription; a story-named query then reports as
a gap exactly as it did before.
_auditNote: The exclusion above is the FIX for a contamination we found. scripts/audit-evidence.ts
is the DETECTOR, and it runs over every root rather than the one that failed:
it hashes each page's Settings blob and compares it against every artifact this
pipeline has written. See evidenceAudit below for what counts as ours.
_excludeComment: Paths inside the roots that are TEST MATERIAL, not evidence.
Athena send a requirement document and its delivered output as a PAIR for us to
test against, and those land inside CLIENT SRC — which is an evidence root. So
within a single `npm test` the extractors had absorbed the answer: delivered page
AttachConsumablesToResource suddenly sourced from the test pair's own output file.
That is circular. A pair exists to answer 'could we have produced this?', and it
cannot answer that once its answer is in the dictionary the generator reads.
Excluded here rather than by moving their folder: the files stay where Athena put
them, and the reason lives in config where a diff shows it rather than in
somebody's memory. The staleness gates are what caught this within minutes — a
silent version would have shown up as a suspiciously good score.

_comment: What counts as OUR OWN output, for scripts/audit-evidence.ts (item 4, F-169).
Three of the pages being counted as client evidence were pages WE generated,
and one of them was sitting under a folder called `input\` reading as a
perfectly legitimate before-the-change baseline. So the audit identifies our
work by CONTENT, not by where it sits.
ourOutputFiles is the load-bearing half. A run directory holds both the
artifacts we wrote and the client files we ran against — a first version of
the audit swept everything under _working/experiment and flagged two of
Athena's own delivered samples as ours, because they sit in experiment/inputs/.
Only the filenames this pipeline WRITES are ours.
Remove this block and the audit falls back to the same four roots and two
filenames, so an older config still behaves identically.
Input guards. Without these a runaway document reaches the model and comes
back as an opaque API error instead of a message the user can act on (T-23).
storyChars MEASURED against the real corpus: Athena's user stories extract to
905 and 1,854 characters, and the largest document they have sent — the
961-paragraph step-by-step build document — is 42,614. 500,000 leaves more
than ten times the headroom over the largest real input while still catching
a 4.5 MB paste, which would be roughly 1.1 million tokens and cannot be sent.
Raise it if a genuine story is ever refused; that is a config edit, not a
code change.
THE INTAKE SEQUENCE, ENFORCED. Requirement document -> the model asks
what it cannot settle -> a PRD the engineer can argue with -> and only
then code.
THIS REVERSES A RECORDED DECISION, and that is deliberate rather than a
drift. LEDGER §8 and §13.9 both say the PRD was put before generation
'without making it a gate', so an engineer who said 'just build it' got
that. The client asked for the flow to be enforced, because a run that
skipped straight to generation produced a page nobody had agreed the
shape of, and the PRD is where the disagreement is supposed to be cheap.
requirePrdBeforeGenerate  generate_artifact is refused until a PRD exists.
requirePrdReview          ...and until the engineer has said something
after it was written. That is a proxy for
'reviewed', and an honest one: it proves they
had the document in front of them and replied.
Set either to false to restore the old behaviour. Remove the block
entirely and the gates are off, so a config written before this still
loads and still behaves as it did.

loop._attemptsNote: attempt 1 plus up to 2 regenerations. Only FAIL findings are fed back; WARN never triggers a retry.

_layoutNote: Page-specific values the skeleton leaves open — NOT platform facts.
columns genuinely varies: 20 / 6 / 10 across Athena's three samples, and
6 (54 pages), 8 (6), 24 (3), 18 (2), 16 (1) across the 66 live pages. 6 is
the mode, so it is the default, but a page that needs another value must say
so (--columns). width is 1024 in all three samples; live pages split
titleFollowsName: definition.title equals the page Name in all three samples
and in 40 of 66 live pages — so it is the default, not a rule. Override
with --title. Every value used is printed on each run; none is applied silently.

postProcess._idsNote: $id is a deterministic function of the JSON structure, so our code assigns it rather than the model. Round 2 emitted 3 markers for 207 objects; arithmetic over 200+ objects is not a judgement task.
